steps.explanation:
An animation is planned from its **key poses**: the extremes of the motion. Everything else is filled in between them later.

This slime breathes by squashing and stretching. Start with the squash: wide and low, its body spread out over the ground.

![Frame 1: squash](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 3: stretch](examples/frame-3.png)

Keep the bottom row on the same ground line in every Frame, so the slime stays put while it moves.

The second key pose is the stretch: narrower and taller than the squash. A slime is soft, so it keeps roughly the same amount of body. What it loses in width it gains in height.

Click Frame 1 in the Frame strip to compare, and check that the bottom row sits on the same ground line as the squash.

![Frame 1: squash](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 3: stretch](examples/frame-3.png)

In-betweens carry the motion from one key pose to the next. This one is on the way up: as wide as the squash at its widest, but one row taller at the top.

Turn on **Onion skin** (O). Frames 1 and 3 sit on either side of this one, so you can see both key poses faintly behind it. Aim between them.

![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 3](examples/frame-3.png)

The last in-between takes the slime from the stretch back down, so the loop runs smoothly from Frame 4 into Frame 1.

It has the same body as Frame 2, but the eyes sit one row higher. Small differences between in-betweens like this keep an idle loop from feeling mechanical.

With Onion skin on you see Frame 3 behind this one. Press **Play preview** (P) to watch the whole loop.

![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 4](examples/frame-4.png)
